opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It was a gradual realization over the first few years of my PhD.

When I started, I worked on algorithms, mostly transfer learning: how to take a pretrained model and adapt it well to downstream tasks. It was a good area and I learned a lot. But around the time large language models started to take off, I felt the ground shifting. Many of the clever algorithmic tricks we spent months on got washed out once models became big enough and were trained on enough data. Scale itself was doing much of the work that we used to try to do with careful algorithm design.

That made me ask: if scale matters this much, what's actually stopping us from going further? More and more, the answer was systems. How do you train these models efficiently? How do you serve them to millions of users without it being ridiculously expensive? Those felt like real, concrete bottlenecks, not things you could tune away with a new loss function.

There was also a personal side. In algorithm research, a lot of papers report a small improvement on a benchmark, and you're not always sure it matters in practice. In systems, the feedback is very direct. Either your code runs faster or it doesn't. Either people use it or they don't. I really liked that honesty. When I started contributing to open-source projects and saw people actually depending on the code I wrote, that was very motivating, much more than another point of accuracy on some dataset.

And I think my algorithm background actually helped. Understanding what the model is doing, why certain operations matter, where the computation goes, makes you a better systems person. So I don't see it as abandoning one field for another. It's more like moving to where I felt I could make the biggest impact at that moment in time.

r001.rationale: The response cites scaling and systems bottlenecks, but does not attribute the choice to limited compute resources in his lab.

r002.rationale: It says model scale could wash out algorithmic improvements, but does not say replacing a pretrained model with a newer, larger one could outperform a year of his algorithm research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, the switch wasn't something I planned from day one. It came out of a kind of frustration that built up gradually.

When I started my PhD, I was working on transfer learning and domain adaptation, which is fairly classic algorithm research. You propose a new loss, a new regularizer, you run experiments, you get a point or two of improvement on some benchmark, and you write a paper. I published several papers that way, and for a while that felt satisfying.

But around the time large models started taking over, I noticed something uncomfortable. A lot of the clever tricks I had worked on simply stopped mattering once you scaled the model and the data up. The gains got washed out. Meanwhile, the thing that actually determined whether a research group could do interesting work was no longer the algorithm idea. It was whether you could train and run the model at all, and how fast and how cheaply you could do it. I'd spend weeks fighting with GPU memory, with distributed training bugs, with inference being too slow to iterate on experiments. And I realized that the people solving those problems were having far more impact than I was with my incremental algorithm papers.

The second trigger was more personal. I spent a lot of time digging into PyTorch internals just to get my own experiments working, and I found that I genuinely enjoyed it. Understanding how the compiler stack works, how the kernels are dispatched, why something is slow, and then fixing it so that everyone downstream benefits. That felt much more concrete to me than another benchmark number. And when I started contributing to open-source systems projects, the feedback loop was immediate. Real users would hit the problem, I'd fix it, and the next day thousands of people were running the faster version.

So it was a combination of those two things. Intellectually, I became convinced that systems were the bottleneck for AI progress, not algorithms. And emotionally, I found that I liked the work more. My advisor was quite supportive, which helped a lot, because a mid-PhD pivot is risky. But looking back, it was the best decision I made during those years.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was a gradual shift. When you work on AI algorithms, you also spend a lot of time getting experiments to run—dealing with memory limits, training speed, and debugging. I became increasingly interested in those problems themselves: why was something slow, and how could we make it work more efficiently?

What appealed to me about machine-learning systems was the broader impact. Improving an algorithm might help with a particular task, while improving the underlying system can help many people develop and run different algorithms. I still cared about AI, but I found myself more drawn to the infrastructure that makes it practical.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was a gradual shift. When I was working on algorithms, I kept running into questions about the systems underneath them: Why was an experiment taking so long? Why wasn’t the GPU being fully utilized? Could we run the same model more efficiently?

I found myself increasingly interested in those questions. An algorithm might look very promising, but you still need a good system to train it, evaluate it, and make it useful in practice. And a systems improvement can benefit many different models, rather than just one particular method.

So I didn’t really see it as leaving AI research. I was moving toward the part of AI research that I enjoyed most—understanding how things actually execute and making them work better.
